paragraphs: I was allowed to study at the Medical University of Vienna for three months. Vienna was a wonderful city full of cultural and historical atmosphere, suggesting that it was the centre of Europe for a long time. The two huge cubes that catch the eye as soon as you come up to street level on subway line 6 are the buildings of the Vienna General Hospital (Allgemeines Krankenhaus, AKH), where I did my clerkship. It is a large hospital, the largest in Europe, with over 2000 beds, and I was able to learn various things.
I rotated through three departments, radiology, transplant surgery and ophthalmology, for one month each.

Radiology was a huge department that handles everything from imaging to image reading to radiation therapy, and its very fine division into sections was impressive. There were extremely many sections, such as chest X-ray, general CT, surgical CT, MRI by body part, and neuroradiology, and each section concentrates on one thing. I strongly felt the difference from Japan in the thorough division of labour and the enormous number of radiology readings. A day began with a conference in the morning, followed by following the doctors of each section. I was also fortunate to have opportunities to state findings and discuss in English.

In transplant surgery, almost all cases were cadaveric transplants and greatly depended on the timing of when a donor appeared (died), so the operations were at midnight or early morning and I often could not take part. For that reason I was also allowed to observe operations in general surgery, which shares the ward and operating rooms. Here too the flow was that after the morning conference, I went to the operating room of an operation I was interested in, asked the doctor, and was allowed to take part. In the operating room they spoke German, but if I asked in English they answered in a friendly manner, and I was even let in to the operative field, so it was a meaningful clerkship.

Ophthalmology, like radiology, had various sections, and among them I think the macula section looked after me most. It is a section that deals with diseases of the macula and retina, centred on age-related macular degeneration, and although the number of patients was large, it was not an extremely busy section. For that reason, I was able to gain a lot of experience, being taught carefully about diseases and treatments from the basics, conducting medical interviews with patients, and, at the end, having my own fundus findings examined in detail and explained to me.
Clerkship, local life, interaction and leisure were all new, stimulating and fulfilling for the three months. I sincerely think it was good that I went.

Finally, I am deeply grateful to Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川 and the other members of the International Collaboration Office who gave me great support over a long period, the doctors who are alumni of the Frontier Association, the doctors of the Medical University of Vienna, and everyone who supported me. Thank you.
